analysis.one_liner: Replaces Clean Air Act power-plant pollution programs with a cap-and-trade system for sulfur dioxide, smog, and mercury.
analysis.headline: Introduced in November 2003 with zero cosponsors, the bill died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never came to a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the Clean Air Act's power-plant programs, replacing plant-by-plant pollution limits with a trading system for sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury from coal- and oil-fired power plants. Plants would receive emission allowances free of charge and could buy more from the government at set prices. It also would have exempted covered plants from certain existing permitting requirements and let operators delay compliance by petitioning the Energy Department on electricity-reliability grounds. It never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of coal- and oil-fired electric generating units. The bill allocated sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury allowances 'without cost to the recipient' [S3], let covered units escape consideration as major emitting facilities for preconstruction review and nonattainment plan requirements [S2], gave owners a petition process for a compliance delay if pollution-control installation might threaten electricity reliability [S2], and let the President temporarily grant waivers from the emission limitations [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal- and oil-fired power plant owners

how_it_helps.text: Allowances for emitting sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury are allocated 'without cost to the recipient' [S3].

The bill excludes units meeting specified particulate-matter limits or operating pollution-control equipment from treatment as major emitting facilities for prevention-of-significant-deterioration review and nonattainment plan requirements [S2].
Owners may petition the Secretary of Energy for a determination that pollution-control installation threatens electricity reliability, winning a compliance delay [S2].
The President may temporarily grant waivers from the emission limitations if national electricity supply or national security is imperiled [S3].
Clean coal technology demonstration projects and reactivated very clean coal units are exempted from certain performance standards and preconstruction review requirements [S3].

The bill sets new performance standards for new boilers, integrated gasification combined cycle plants, and combustion turbines, and requires EPA research on particulate matter and mercury effects [S2].

analysis.who_pays: People living near and downwind of power plants, who bear whatever pollution remains under the caps and any hot spots created by trading; and states, which would lose some ability to impose their own emissions increases restrictions beyond what the bill prescribes [S2]. Because the excess-emissions penalty is calibrated to the market price of allowances [S3], a plant that finds cleaning up more expensive than buying or buying allowances can simply pay to pollute, and the cost of that pollution falls on surrounding communities.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near and downwind of power plants

drawbacks.text: The excess-emissions penalty for units under the new programs is calculated at the annual average market price of allowances [S3], which means the bill's own enforcement mechanism prices pollution rather than prohibiting it; a plant can exceed its limits and pay.

Mercury, a pollutant that accumulates in fish and wildlife, becomes tradeable in one-ounce allowances [S3]. Trading a persistent toxic pollutant can concentrate emissions around plants that buy allowances instead of installing controls, creating local hot spots even when the national cap is met — a mechanism critics of the design have long pointed to.

Covered units are excluded from major-source preconstruction review and certain nonattainment-area plan requirements [S2], removing a check that today requires new or modified major sources to install the best available control technology and analyze community air-quality impacts before building.
The reliability petition process and presidential waiver allow delays or suspensions of the emission limitations themselves [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does mandate real reductions — new caps and allowance programs for sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury, plus performance standards for new plants [S2]. But its design trades enforceable plant-level obligations for a market system: allowances are free, the penalty for over-emitting equals the market price of an allowance, and covered units get relief from several existing permitting requirements. Whether the caps would have produced deeper or shallower cuts than the programs it replaced was the central dispute over the proposal, and it never got far enough for that dispute to be tested in a vote. On its face, the structure shifts discretion from regulators and states to plant owners holding allowances.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced, and it sat there with no markup, no floor action, and no vote through the end of the 108th Congress [S5].

narrative.text: Sen. James Inhofe introduced S. 1844, the Clear Skies Act of 2003, on November 10, 2003 [S1][S5].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing outcome, markup, or floor vote recorded in the action history, and the 108th Congress ended January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo won. Because the bill died, coal- and oil-fired plant owners never received the free allowances, permitting exemptions, or delay mechanisms it offered, and the existing Clean Air Act programs it would have replaced stayed in force. Environmental and public-health opponents of the bill achieved their goal without needing a vote, since its own sponsor never moved it out of committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Supporters of the existing Clean Air Act

for.name: Sen. James Inhofe
for.role: Senator from Oklahoma and Chairman, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the Clear Skies Act of 2003; as the committee's chairman, never brought it to a markup or floor vote.

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Proposed the 'Clear Skies' initiative and backed legislation implementing it.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral; no markup or vote was ever reported.

against.name: Sen. James Jeffords
against.role: Senator from Vermont and ranking member of the Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Opposed the Clear Skies approach and championed competing legislation with deeper, faster pollution cuts.

against.name: Environmental and public health groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill as weaker and slower than existing Clean Air Act programs, particularly on mercury.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by the Republican committee chairman but attracted zero cosponsors of either party [S4], so no party bloc ever took a recorded position on it.

industries.note: The bill hands affected generating units free emission allowances for sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury [S3], exempts covered units from major-source preconstruction review [S2], and offers compliance delays through reliability petitions [S2]. The value comes from replacing existing plant-by-plant obligations with a trading system whose permits to pollute cost nothing up front.

The bill builds its allocation formulas around coal-fired units' historical heat input and includes clean coal technology regulatory incentives [S3], supporting continued coal-based generation rather than fuel switching.

A cap-and-trade system lets plants meet limits by buying allowances instead of installing scrubbers and other controls [S3], shrinking the market for equipment these companies sell. Communities benefit only to the extent plants actually cut emissions rather than buy allowances.
